# Introduction
'Mobility hub' is a relatively new term 
for locations where a range of transport modes, 
especially transit and shared micro-mobility, 
and sometimes other services and facilities 
are offered. 
These might provide 
a range of 
non-private-or-petrol-driven-car alternatives 
that might help towards 
more sustainable travel behaviours and transport system outcomes. 
Nearby shared electric cars, 
bikes and cargo-bikes, 
e-bikes and e-cargo bikes, 
or other vehicles 
might help in shifting towards 
more walking, cycling and transit-based travel 
through providing options for those,
more occasional, 
trips that are otherwise difficult without a car, 
(e.g. travelling with luggage, 
longer distances 
or outside typical service times). 
A nearby mobility hub 
might allow households to
forgo purchase of 
a(n additional) car, 
or transition to electrically-powered modes 
without the upfront expense. 
Some mobility hubs, 
such as those in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) in Canada, 
are defined as such by a regional transport authority, 
with implications for landuse planning 
and other institutional decision-making \citep{Salsberg:2010aa, Engel-Yan:2012aa}. 
Others are created afresh, 
through some agency 
implementing facilities 
for a range of modes and/or other offerings 
in close proximity to each other 
and with branding as a 'mobility hub' or similar. 

In some cases 
it may be that a range of offerings are already in place, 
especially where the private sector has already implemented 
car-, scooter-, bike- or other -share services. 
Converting such places into a 'mobility hub' 
may be within reach with just a mobility-hub-related name, 
a press-release or website, 
and perhaps some minimal physical interventions such as signage and advertising. 
However, tools for transforming such locations 
into 'mobility hubs' 
do not yet appear to be readily available. 
Instead, individual agencies implementing mobility hubs 
appear to have been largely created 
signage, advertising and similar elements 
afresh and bespoke by on a site-by-site basis, 
albeit that some hubs created in groups 
appear to have similar branding and designs. 
Such creation might involve graphic design, mapping or similar 
and so limit the opportunities for 
trials, 
bottom-up implementation 
or other low-cost interventions 
by practitioners or 
(potentially through tactical urbanism and/or grassroots activism) 
sustainability-focused advocates or other actors.

This paper reports findings from case and design-based research 
seeking to develop new tools to support low-cost mobility hub implementation. 
The research adopts the Double Diamond Design process 
and iterates through 
alternatively diverging and coverging 
phases of Discovery, Definition, Development and Delivery 
(c.f. \cite{UK-Design-Council:0aa}). 
Exploratory field visits to a range of case study mobility hubs 
help inform the Discovery and Development phases, 
while a new package of software tools 
to support mapping and the 
generation of informational signage and other physical interventions 
forms the key research outcome 
from the Delivery phase. 
This software might allow practitioners or others to
create a temporary mobility hub on a trial basis, 
or as the first step towards designing and implementing 
more permanent information and mapping. 
The rest of this paper is structured as follows: 
the next section outlines the context for this research, 
including brief discussion of mobility hubs and tactical urbanism. 
The research methodology is then described, 
followed by presentation of the results, 
which are then briefly discussed 
in conjunction with a conclusion identifying directions for future research.  

# Research context
Mobility hubs are an emerging approach 
where shared and micro-mobility offerings, 
transit 
or other offerings are linked 
to provide a range of options that support more sustainable travel. 
Early use of the term occured in Toronto, Canada, 
as part of landuse and transport planning undertaken by Metrolinx 
and other governmental institutions 
across the surrounding region \citep{Salsberg:2010aa, Engel-Yan:2012aa}. 
In "The Big Move" \citep{Metrolinx:2008aa} 
various transit stations and major interchanges were defined as 
"mobility hubs" for the purposes of supporting regional travel, 
modal interchange, 
and transitions to more transit supportive landuse patterns. 

The plethora of independent private-sector transport offerings 
now available, 
including car-share and dockless bike/scooter systems, 
may also have helped towards development of the mobility hub concept. 
Although driven largely by 
start-up, technology and communications, and related sectors, 
various governmental agencies have sought to both: 
regulate such offerings; 
and make them more than the sum of their parts. 
Defining dockless parking locations, 
allocating dedicated carshare parking spaces, 
installation of branding and informational signage 
and similar efforts 
may help to 
provide geo-spatial context and collectivisation. 
As well, there have been some emerging problems, 
including with respect to inappropriate parking of 
dockless bikes/scooters (i.e. blocking footpaths), 
and risks 
and environmental impacts 
of recharging models 
that rely on batteries being collected and then charged elsewhere, 
often without the appropriate facilities 
to deal with electrical loads or battery fires \citep{Meigs:2023aa, Zhang:2022aa}. 
Shared electric mobility hubs, 
such as those currently being trialled in Ireland as part of the ROBUST project \citep{ROBUST:2025aa}, 
may provide solutions to such problems 
by shifting the recharging of vehicles to be at a hub itself 
where appropriate parking, electrical connections and other equipment 
(importantly for fires involving lithium batteries) are outside 
and typically unenclosed.

Other challenges
for implementers and communities, however, 
may relate to the difficulty of developing mobility hubs, 
including the planning processes and funding acquisition necessary 
to build new facilities. 
Of course, 
other than the name 
there may be nothing new about mobility hubs - 
railway stations have existing for over a century. 
Often containing 
waiting areas and information, 
cafes, 
parking lots, 
interchange with other modes such as buses, 
and many other facilities 
the 19th, 20th and current iterations of railway stations 
would appear to have largely already 'solved', 
many of the problems related to how to 
support mobility at a network hub 
(albeit that these solutions might not always be fully implemented). 
However, stations tend to be located on land owned 
or otherwise controlled by railway companies or agencies. 
As such, 
facilities, 
signage, 
branding, 
information displays 
and most other aspects of the station environment 
might be largely under the control of a single institution, 
or only a small number of closely-related agencies. 
Mobility hubs, in contrast, 
might tend to be located in public road reserves, 
within parking facilities or otherwise 
where there may be less clear authority and power to make changes 
without widespread public, institutional and government approvals or buy-in. 
These may also often require outside expertise 
and/or involve top-down policy-making 
in which those making decisions might be somewhat removed 
from the real mobility needs of individual communities, 
or who may adopt 'one size fits all' approaches 
lacking responsiveness to local context. 

Research in public policy analysis has long been examining on such non-rational factors
and how they might influence decision-making, 
but these tend to be overlooked in transport policy research \citep{Marsden:2017aa}. 
Instutionalism, 
political approaches, 
incrementalism and other public policy models, 
however, 
are clearly applicable to transport systems (see for example \citet{Reynolds:2017ah}). 
Important within these are the top-down, bottom-up and hybrid theories of implementation, 
which emphasise the influence that street-level bureaucrats can wield 
to obtain outcomes that respond to their local needs and context, 
including sometimes outcomes 
that might be in opposition to central policy directions. 
Further exploration of this topic may be beyond the scope of this paper, 
but the extensive body of research related to the Advocacy Coalition Framework (including \citet{Sabatier:1986aa,Sabatier:1987aa,Sabatier:1988aa,Sabatier:1993aa,Weible:2009aa,Weible:2007aa}) provides insights and theory.  

Perhaps of more relevance, however, is the field of tactical urbanism, 
which adopts many such bottom-up and grassroots approaches 
to defining and re-imaging public spaces, 
especially those spaces 
within road reserves and related to transport systems. 
Tactical urbanism 
can involve making changes to public environments, 
often unsanctioned, 
that sometimes question what urban space is for 
or the legitimacy of how it is allocated. 
"PARKing Day" provides an example, 
having started as lunchtime take over of an on-street car parking space 
by an architecture firm, 
who rolled out some green grass and a park bench, 
paid the parking meter, 
and in doing so questioned the validity of using such spaces 
for storing vehicles instead of as a parklet for people. 
This has since grown into an annual event seeking, 
like the World Naked Bike Ride and Critical Mass, 
to demonstrate the possibility of change and question the legitimacy of the (car-dominated) status quo 
\citep{Lydon:2012aa,Davidson:2013aa,Lydon:2015aa,Blumgart:2016ab, Ride:2009aa, Morhayim:2012aa, Longhurst:2015aa}. 
Similar 'pop-up' or protest-based approaches 
have helped legitimise bicycle lanes, 
delegitimise car-use of bus lanes, 
and are sometimes used as more mainstream 
ways (amongst engineers and planners) 
to help build public and institutional support for implementation, 
including for the installation of transit lanes \citep{Fucoloro:2013aa,News:2019ab, TransitCenter:2018ab, Transportation-Studies:2019aa}. 
These build on or have similarities to various earlier approaches 
including street-reclaiming 
\citep{Dobson:2023ae,Engwicht:1999aa,Fotel:2009aa,Institute:2015aa}, 
the invention of the first 'woornef' \citep{Guttenberg:1982aa, Lydon:2015aa} 
and Local Area Traffic Management \citep{Damen:2017aa}, 
as well as being evident in the make up of current directions 
towards 'Movement and Place', 'Complete Streets' 
and Network Operation Planning approaches \citep{Delbosc:2018aa}.  

Despite the many names, 
variations and focii of these 
and other interventional and decision-making approaches, 
the call from \citet{Marsden:2017aa} 
to "pay greater attention to context,
politics, power, resources and legitimacy" 
retains relevance. 
Participating in unsanctioned activities, 
especially for minorities or others 
who might attract higher levels of attention from authorities, 
can be a risk that might limit engagement 
in tactical urbanism or similar activities \citep{Douglas:2018aa}. 
Intersections between illegality, illegitimacy and the ill-enforced 
similarly exist in the context of street art and its place on a continuum 
that includes commissioned murals, 
counter-culturism and the \emph{avant-garde}, 
graffiti and vandalism. 
\citet{Killen:2017aa,Killen:2021aa} explore these topics 
in the context of trains, but 
of relevance here, however,
are questions relating to who is allowed to post 
a public notice, 
define a 'mobility hub' 
or otherwise share knowledge about transport options, 
local facilities and services, and connecting modes. 

Engineers, planners, operational managers, communications teams 
and others 
may have less need to engage in tactical-urbanist-type implementation 
given that they might already have legitimate authority 
to make changes to the built environment, 
at least within the scope of their employment and remit. 
However, pop-ups, trials, bottom-up and incremental approaches to implementation 
may still be of use, or even necessary, 
for such actors when seeking legitimacy for 
new, unusual or just controversial interventions. 
\citet{Reynolds:2020aa,Reynolds:2021ab} define these 
as 'pragmatic strategies for legitimation *through* implementation' 
based on case research of such approaches helping in the implementation of 
Bus Rapid Transit in Curitiba 
and other forms of transit priority in Zurich, Melbourne and Toronto. 
Other strategies include building legitimacy *before* implementation 
using technical evaluation, vision-based planning 
and/or public decision-making processes; 
or avoiding impacts on those who might seek to delegitimise change. 

Basic signage, linemarking or the public display of travel information 
would appear likely to be relatively easy for many practitioners 
to implement within their own institutional setting. 
What may be lacking, however, are tools and standarised approaches 
to mobility hub information provision 
for quick and relatively easy adaptation to local contexts. 
Likewise, for activists, 
practitioners wishing to affect change 
outside the remit of their specific employment suituation, 
or the general public there do not appear to be tools 
that might support tactical urbanism efforts related to mobility hubs. 
This might be particularly relevant for the 'creation' of a mobility hub 
out of already existing and geographically-proximate facilitates, 
which might not be immediately obvious to travellers 
but something 
informally well-known and readily apparent 
to those with local knowledge of the geography and community. 
Leaflets, 
posters for shop windows and community noticeboards, 
or even resources 
for a tactical urbanist to launch a 'guerilla marketing' campaign 
of posters, Do-It-Yourself (DIY) signage and websites, 
might be all that is needed to facilitiate bottom-up action 
and empower communities to define their own hubs 
and advertise their pre-existing mobility services and related facilities.

What appears to be lacking in the research literature, 
or in practice, 
are the tools to quickly and easily 
produce the sorts of maps, analysis and interpretations 
that might support the definition of a place as a hub 
and the communciation of its existing and potential mobility and other offerings. 
Mapping, signage and similar interventions 
in both the physical and virtual 
might usually tend to be produced on a bespoke 
(ie. location-by-location) basis 
by specialist geographers and graphic designers, 
and involve commercially-controlled datasets or platforms. 
With the advent of crowd-sourcing, 
open data and the widespread availability of open source software, however, 
there is the possibilty of developing location-bespoke, but generalised, 
mapping and similar tools 
useful for practitioners or others wishing to 'mobility hub-erise' 
some part of the urban environment. 
The methods used in this research 
to firstly define what such tools might do, 
and then to deliver a software package 
that enables others to more easily develop their own mobility hub mapping and informational materials, 
which might provide an initial version for future refinement, 
are therefore descrbed in the following.


# Methodology

\citet{Coxon:2018aa,Coxon:2021ab} outline 
various industrial design approaches and tools, 
as well as discussing their relevance and potential applicability 
to transport systems. 
Notable amongst these is the Double Diamond, 
which involves iteration across 
four phases alternating between: 
diverging (1) Discovery 
and then converging (2) Definition phases; 
followed by diverging (3) Development 
and convergence to (4) Delivery of a design output \citep{UK-Design-Council:0aa}. 
This study adopts this approach 
together with case studies of existing mobility hubs. 

Case studies can be especially effective
when theory development is at an early stage 
and when there is a need to explore phenomena within real-world contexts, 
as is the situation here. 
A challenge, however, 
is the need to be seeking generalisable findings 
despite researching at depth within the case contexts.
Such depth is possible through including only a small number of cases, 
typically up to five to ten, 
yet leads to the suggestion that researchers should explictly respond to this "duality criterion" \citep{Benbasat:1987aa,Eisenhardt:1989aa,Dyer:1991aa,Cavaye:1996aa,Darke:1998aa,Meredith:1998aa,Stuart:2002aa,Voss:2002aa,Denscombe:2007aa,Eisenhardt:2007aa,Yin:2009ab,Ketokivi:2014aa,Yin:2014ab,Yin:2018ab}. Here the need to be seeking generalisable findings 
is addressed directly 
by the form taken by outputs, namely: 
the research produces a software of package tools 
for mobility hubs in any location, 
not just those selected as cases.

Hubs were visited in London^[South Woodford and High Street Wanstead; and in Camden: Charrington Street, Goldington Crescent, Werrington Street, Cranlegith Street, Brill Place, Doric Way and Chalton Street.], Bristol^[Abbey Wood, UWE Frenchay, Horfield Library and Gainsborough Square] and Brimingham^[Huntingtree Park and Andrew Road]. 
Case selection for this study was somewhat constrained 
by logistics of travel, meaning that visited sites were in the south of England.
However, and in line with the recommendations of the methodological literature, 
the cases selected included leading and particularly novel examples, 
those that are more representative, 
and sufficient variation to provide for cross-case comparison. 
Cases were selected from a larger sample available at https://www.como.org.uk/mobility-hubs/built-and-planned-hubs.

The findings from site visits 
where synthesised through cross-case comparison 
to develop the design problem Definition. 
The Development was guided by standardised approaches to package development 
for the R language, 
using @wickham2023r as a key reference. 
R is chosen here because: 
it is open source and freely available, 
therefore supporting goals of developing an accessible suite of tools; 
it has an extensive set of packages for geospatial analysis and mapping, 
including *sf* [@R-sf], 
and the *osmdata* [@R-osmdata] packages; 
and there is a large community of users 
who might help support those with less experience in troubleshooting, 
but who are also responsible 
for the development and maintenance of a wide range of packages, 
including: the *tidyverse* [@tidyverse2019] and many others 
used in code development for this research.

Information panels, maps and other guides to facitilies and services were present at some hubs, but notably not at those in Camden, South Woodford or High Street Wanstead. These locations were all in London, however, and generally close to already existing maps and other information at tube stations, bus stops or  otherwise provided, which may have lessened the need for mobility-hub-specific signage and mapping. Figures \ref{fig:andrew_road_images} and \ref{fig:bristol_images_panels} show selected images of informational panels and signage found at the hubs in Birmingham and Bristol, 
which shared some common design elements such as including both local and area-wide maps, icongraphic representation of facilities, and directional information. Notably, the Bristol hubs included green cubes mounted overhead hub facilities, which appear likely to assist in finding hub elements in busy urban environments. 
Mapping and informational material, however, 
often appeared to include some that are not specifically 'part' of a hub 
(e.g. toliets within anouther facilities, shops, cafes). 
This highlights a potential question for implementers: 
what services and facilities to include as 'part of the hub', versus those that are just 'nearby'? 
In the case of the Transport for West Midlands hub at Andrew Road 
(Figure \ref{fig:andrew_road_images})
directional signage to, 
and information about, 
bus services 
at the nearby Halesowen Bus Station (approx 50m walking distance) 
is provided, 
but the hub has a different location-based name and branding identity. 

Some of the hubs included linemarked areas 
for shared e-bike, e-scooter or e-cargobike parking, 
bicycle parking and secure parking lockers, 
although the offered facilities and services varied by location.
A lack of shade, 
weather protection and drinking water 
was also evident at most of the visited hubs, 
even though many of the parklet-type facilities 
included steel framing that might have accommodated open-sided roofing or similar.
This might indicate an emphasis on form over function in some 
design elements,
whereas one of the hubs in Bristol 
perhaps provides an example of additional functionality 
- a containerised "Library of Things" - 
that appears to have been added later into the hub area,
onto top of areas linemarked and sign-posted as for electric scooter hire. 
This may provide an indication of the possibilities 
of using modular components to expand, 
re-purpose or adjust mobility hubs as situations change 
(consistent with \citet{Stuart:2002aa}), 
but a need for signs and 
maps to be easily adjustable to match, 
as updating such elements might relatively challenging for practitioners, 
location managers or others once 
the original graphic designers or implementers have moved on^[See also \citet{Reynolds:2017ah} discussion of 'The Garbage Can Model'.].   

Overall, the site visits undertaken during the 'Discovery' phase highlight the following key issues: 
design elements; 
included facilities and hub identity; 
and the ability for supporting material 
to be adjusted to changing circumstances. 
Design elements relate to the 
desirability of functional and clearly-related hub components, 
and appears interlinked clarifying 
what types of nearby facilities should be 'part' of the hub 
in terms of branding and 
information^[i.e. Which elements recieve 'green cube' markers in the real world,  
versus which are just an icon on a map?]. 
Identity, likewise, appears to interlinked 
with hub naming - for example, 
the Andrew Road hub is named after 
a relatively less important connector road 
rather than consolidated to be part of the Halesowen bus station.  
As well the site visits 
perhaps also highlighted the importance of 
maintenance, 
activity^[c.f. \citet{Jacobs:1961aa} "eye on the street"] 
and updates to match changing circumstances 
that might give a hub a sense of 'place'. 
Hubs in Bristol 
perhaps provide an example
with litter, 
non-mobility-related signage, 
space requisitioned for other purposes, 
and some sites advertising dockless shared vehicles 
but without these present in sufficient numbers 
(or at all at the time of visiting Gainsborough Square) 
all providing indications of potential post-implementation challenges 
related to mobility hubs.  

## Definition

Findings from the sites visits suggest 
a wide variety of modes, services and facilities
might be provided as part of the hub itself, 
as well as further services and facilities 
identified as being 'nearby' 
as an extension of the hub offer. 
This might suggest adopting an open-ended 
and expansionist approach to mobility hub definition. 

The consistency of branding at the Bristol hubs, 
especially with respect to the iconographic green cubes 
drawing attention to hub elements, 
might highlight the importance of proximity 
and line-of-sight in defining a mobility hub. 
Although mapping at most hubs provided information 
about services and facilities within up to around 15 minutes walking distance, 
hub elements appeared to generally be located within relatively confined areas, 
generally spanning less than 50 metres. 
The Andrew Road hub provides an example 
towards the upper end,
with the entirety of the hub and the nearby Halesown Bus Station 
encompassed within a radius of approximately 70 metres, 
and spanning slightly less than 200 metres if traversed by foot. 
In contrast, the South Woodford hub 
takes up approximately 15 metres of kerb space 
and is less than 100 metres from the nearest tube station, 
while some in Camden use space equivalent to only a few car parking spots. 

Definitions of the facilities, 
services and modes necessary 
to become a mobility hub appear 
likewise to be open-ended and inclusive, 
rather than some sort of minimum checklist that all sites must have^[CoMoUK's 
pop-up mobility hub offering provide an example, 
with the basic option consisting of a 12 square metre parklet 
with bike repair facilitates, 
and bike parking and/or bike share docking \citep{CoMoUK:0aa}.]. 
In *Mobility hub delivery models* \cite{CoMoUK:2021aa} 
discuss six types of mobility hubs: 
"large interchanges/city hubs...; 
transport corridor, smaller interchanges or linking hubs; 
business park or new housing development hubs; 
suburb/mini-hubs; 
small market town/village hubs; 
and tourism hubs"
along with suggested components for each. 
Further types might included the 'shared' and 'electric' forms of mobility hub, 
as in the ROBUST sites, 
wherein the offered modes are 
available for hire 
and electrically powered respectively. 
It is unclear, however, 
whether there is a need to differentiate between electric hubs (or 'e-hubs') 
where the electrification involves on-site recharging, 
as at ROBUST and for many e-cars, 
and hubs where electric vehicles are dockless or otherwise 'recharged' 
through the replacement of battery packs with those powered up elsewhere. 


Guidance from \cite{CoMoUK:0ab} suggests a timeline of 12 to 15 months 
to step through 
consultation, design, stakeholder engagement, tendering and construction, 
although this appears to relate to either unpowered mobility hubs 
or replacable batteries. 
This guidance also suggests that budgets i
n the vicinity of 250k to 650k pounds \cite{CoMoUK:0ac}; 
and that 
"mobility hubs work best when part of a wider sustainable transport network 
that provides  active travel, public transport and shared transport options" \cite{CoMoUK:0aa}. 
The design problem here, therefore, 
appears be to allow creation of mobility hubs that: 
incorporate existing modes, facilities and services; 
minimise cost and timeframes, 
such that practitioners and tactical urbanists 
might build legitimacy through implementation (c.f. \cite{Reynolds:2020aa,Reynolds:2021ab}) 
using minimal resources, 
incremental approaches that allow expansion one-hub-at-a-time, 
and that are scaleable; 
and allow for rapid iteration, 
revision or adjustment to account for changing circumstances. 
There are limits, however, 
to what can be achieved in the context of this research study, 
suggesting that the focus here should be on designing tools 
that allow for mobility hub creation 
without the sorts of 'hard' engineering works that would necessitate design,
tendering and construction of new facilities or infrastructure.  
Rather, this research defines the design problem to be solved 
as to create software tools that might facilitate 
the creation and rapid development of user information products 
to support bottom-up, tactical urbanist and iterative approaches.  


## Development

Both the Andrew Road and various Bristol mobility hubs feature pedestal-mounted signage that includes: the hub name; iconographic representations of hub facilities; directional indications; and two maps. These maps are, respectively, of the local vicinity (a 5-10 minute walk) of the hub; and the surrounding area (a 15-20 minute walk). A starting point for developing software packages to support creation of further mobility hubs, therefore, would appear to be outputting similar maps of the local and surrounding areas, composited together into a image of similar size to the pedestal signage encountered during the site visits along with site naming and other information.

```{r extract_osm_data_bristol, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE }
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%

                  )

                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
                    st_bbox()
                  )
### based on https://github.com/ropensci/osmdata/blob/main/vignettes/query-split.Rmd

split_bbox <- function (bbox, grid = 2, eps = 0.05) {
    xmin <- bbox ["x", "min"]
    ymin <- bbox ["y", "min"]
    dx <- (bbox ["x", "max"] - bbox ["x", "min"]) / grid
    dy <- (bbox ["y", "max"] - bbox ["y", "min"]) / grid

    bboxl <- list ()

    for (i in 1:grid) {
        for (j in 1:grid) {
            b <- matrix (c (
                xmin + ((i - 1 - eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j - 1 - eps) * dy),
                xmin + ((i + eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j + eps) * dy)
            ),
            nrow = 2,
            dimnames = dimnames (bbox)
            )

            bboxl <- append (bboxl, list (b))
        }
    }
    bboxl
}

bb_vector <- place_sf[[1]] %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric()
bb <- data.frame(min = bb_vector[1:2], max = bb_vector[3:4])
rownames(bb) <- c("x", "y")               
                 
queue <- split_bbox (bb)
result <- list ()

while (length (queue) > 0) {

    print (queue [[1]])

    opres <- NULL
    opres <- try ({
        opq (bbox = queue [[1]], timeout = 25) |>
            add_osm_feature (key = "building") |>
            osmdata_sf ()
    })

    if (class (opres) [1] != "try-error") {
        result <- append (result, list (opres))
        queue <- queue [-1]
    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}
final_building <- do.call (c, result)
list.save(final_building, "data/bristol_buildings_260608.rdata")

### amenity

result_amenity <- list ()

    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}

final_amenity <- do.call (c, result_amenity)


list.save(final_amenity, "~/data/bristol_amenity_260608.rdata")
```

```{r create_local_map, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.fullwidth = TRUE, out.width= "100%"}
        label = name, geometry = geometry), 
    text.colour = "black", stat = "sf_coordinates", size = 3) +
# TARGET building amenities  
  geom_sf(data = buildings[[i]] %>% filter(amenity %in% target) %>% st_filter(
    poly_as_metres, .predicate =  st_intersects), mapping = aes(), 
    fill = "purple") + 
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = buildings[[i]] %>% filter(
    amenity %in% target) %>% st_filter(
      poly_as_metres, .predicate =  st_intersects), mapping = aes(
        label = name, geometry = geometry), 
    text.colour = "black", stat = "sf_coordinates", size = 3) +
  
 
  ### Walking radius
    geom_sf_label(data = data.frame(xlim = c(mean(xlim - 250)), ylim =c(ylim[2] - 100)) %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("xlim", "ylim"), crs = crs_local_metres) %>%  
  st_as_sfc(), aes(), label = "5 minute walk", colour = "black", angle = 35) +
  theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(), 
        axis.text.x=element_blank(), #remove x axis labels
        axis.ticks.x=element_blank(), #remove x axis ticks
        axis.text.y=element_blank(),  #remove y axis labels
        axis.ticks.y=element_blank(), #remove y axis ticks
        legend.position="none",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8), 
        legend.title = element_blank(), 
        legend.key.size = unit(0.5, 'in'),
        ) + 
  geom_sf(data = hub_location_metres[[i]], size = 8, colour = "red") + 
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = hub_location_metres[[i]], mapping = aes(
      label = "You are here", size = 7, geometry = geometry), 
    stat = "sf_coordinates") + 
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(location = 'br') + 
  ggspatial::annotation_north_arrow() +
  coord_sf(xlim = (poly_as_lat_long %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric() %>% as_tibble() %>% slice(1,3) %>% unlist() %>% as.numeric()),
  ylim = (poly_as_lat_long %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric() %>% as_tibble() %>% slice(2,4) %>% unlist() %>% as.numeric()), crs = 4326) 


}
```

```{r mock_up_layout_with_maps, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Mockup of hub signage. Source: authors.", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("graphics/dundrum_mock_up.png") 


addImg <- function(
  obj, # an image file imported as an array (e.g. png::readPNG, jpeg::readJPEG)
  x = NULL, # mid x coordinate for image
  y = NULL, # mid y coordinate for image
  width = NULL, # width of image (in x coordinate units)
  interpolate = TRUE # (passed to graphics::rasterImage) A logical vector (or scalar) indicating whether to apply linear interpolation to the image when drawing. 
){
  if(is.null(x) | is.null(y) | is.null(width)){stop("Must provide args 'x', 'y', and 'width'")}
  USR <- par()$usr # A vector of the form c(x1, x2, y1, y2) giving the extremes of the user coordinates of the plotting region
  PIN <- par()$pin # The current plot dimensions, (width, height), in inches
  DIM <- dim(obj) # number of x-y pixels for the image
  ARp <- DIM[1]/DIM[2] # pixel aspect ratio (y/x)
  WIDi <- width/(USR[2]-USR[1])*PIN[1] # convert width units to inches
  HEIi <- WIDi * ARp # height in inches
  HEIu <- HEIi/PIN[2]*(USR[4]-USR[3]) # height in units
  rasterImage(image = obj, 
    xleft = x-(width/2), xright = x+(width/2),
    ybottom = y-(HEIu/2), ytop = y+(HEIu/2), 
    interpolate = interpolate)
}
```

Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_layout_with_maps_grob_output} shows output software developed during this research, which uses Open Streets Map (OSM) data sets and mapping tiles to generate a mobility hub information panel.  Here the software has been used to create output for the Galway ROBUST e-mobility hub, although as an example the 'surrounding area map' shown is for the Letterkenny ROBUST hub location so as to demonstrate the generalisability of the research outcomes. 
Key features of the developed software include the ability to highlight points of interest: in Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_layout_with_maps_grob_output} various religious and medical buildings are highlighted in purple, while the library is shown in blue and nearby schools in orange. This is largely similar to the approach used in the maps discovered during the site visits, but might allow considerable flexibility for practitioners in choosing between colours, iconography or other symbols. A powerful aspect of adopting the OSM datasets and an automated approach for creating maps is that settings can be adjusted by the user and new maps generated within minutes.  For example, the 'surrounding area map' shown in Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_layout_with_maps_grob_output} a slightly different OSM tile option is selected, and buildings recorded as "pubs" (rather than public buildings) are shown in blue.

```{r create_area_map_small, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.fullwidth = TRUE, out.width= "100%"}
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = hub_location_metres[[i]], mapping = aes(
      label = "You are here", size = 3, geometry = geometry), 
    stat = "sf_coordinates") + 
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(location = 'br') + 
  ggspatial::annotation_north_arrow() +
  coord_sf(xlim = (poly_as_lat_long %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric() %>% as_tibble() %>% slice(1,3) %>% unlist() %>% as.numeric()),
  ylim = (poly_as_lat_long %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric() %>% as_tibble() %>% slice(2,4) %>% unlist() %>% as.numeric()), crs = 4326) 


}

  
ggsave("graphics/letterkenny_map_small.png", map_area[[1]], width = 3, height = 3, units = "in")
ggsave("graphics/galway_map_small.png", map_area[[2]], width = 3, height = 3, units = "in")
ggsave("graphics/waterford_map_small.png", map_area[[3]], width = 3, height = 3, units = "in")
ggsave("graphics/dublin_map_small.png", map_area[[4]], width = 3, height = 3, units = "in")
```

```{r mock_up_small, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Immediate hub vicinity mockup. Source: authors.", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
knitr::include_graphics("graphics/galway_map_small.png") 



```


Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_small} further demonstrates the flexibility of this approach in presenting an 'immediate vicinity' map of the Galway hub. At this or similarly small scales it might be possible to include individual hub elements (i.e. the e-bikes or car share vehicles) so that users can locate the various services and facilities.  This represents an extension of the mapping approaches seen in the site visits, and might perhaps remove the need for signage or other physical elements to mark the location of hub elements (e.g. the green cubes in Bristol). As well, at this scale individual elements of the surrounding environment may be more readily apparent to hub users.  In Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_small} the mapping tiles show individual pedestrian footpaths. However, as these and other layers can be obtained from OSM these and other 
features might similarly be mapped, coloured or otherwise highlighted if desired.

# Discussion and conclusions

This design-based research has developed a basic suite of mapping and publication software tools that might be used in the context of mobility hubs. The general format and styling is largely based on elements in place at various mobility hubs in Bristol, but as discussed above the flexibility of R might allow users to adjust layouts, styling and other details as desired. Another area in which the developed approach appears to provide advantages is due to the use of OSM data.  As well as being freely available, the OSM online platform allows this dataset to be edited by anyone, and there exists a large community of users who contribute, edit and otherwise maintain this information. In using this dataset this research may assist towards generalisability and use of the study outputs by practitioners in that the OSM database is accessible and has worldwide coverage.  As well, because the OSM dataset is user-editable it may be possible for those who use the outputs of this research to make corrections and additions as appropriate, thereby providing an improved dataset for both the purposes of mobility hub implementation and for other users or use cases. For example, updating data in OSM for the building immediately north-east of the Westside Public Library (Figure \ref{fig:mock_up_small}) might allow that building's name to be displayed on a mobility-hub-related map, yet also add to the completeness of the OSM dataset overall.  

Clearly, there are many avenues for further research in this area. The software might be expanded to automate the production of websites, posters, banners, leaflets and other informational products that might be generated quickly by practitioners, adovocates or others, and so easily maintained and updated. There might be opportunities to develop more generic materials for other purposes, for example: maintenance schedules, inspection logs, management resources and other items that might help a mobility hub 'product owner' facilitate operations, continuance and growth. Further development of 'best practices' in mobility hub informational provision might involve additional case studies, especially of non-UK sites, as well as improvements to the base 'hub signage mockup' developed here (e.g. additional text, implementation of symbolic mapping for facilities such as toilets, groceries and cafes, etc.). Furthermore, there may be a need to better understand what facilities and services might best be included as 'part' of a hub, as opposed to those that are mapped as being 'nearby'. More immediately, user testing and further development of the software, and of the software outputs, especially the maps, would seem an important direction for further research efforts in the short term.  

This paper's title asked a question related to the applicability of tactical urbanist approaches to the topic of mobility hubs.  Underlying this may be larger questions related to 'what is a mobility hub' and 'who gets to define and advertise something as being a mobility hub'. Perhaps every railway station, bus or tram stop, shared or micro-mobility facilities or many other places are *already* mobility hubs, but just no one has put up a sign or handed out a leaflet that designates this as being the case? There may be  laws and other impediments limiting the ability of many people to adopt a DIY attitude to designating, advertising or informing others about how somewhere might already be, or have the potential to be, a mobility hub. Where these are less of an issue, however, it is suggested that with the software developed through this research and access to plotting devices, especially those capable of outputing larger size materials (e.g. A0, A1), almost anyone might be able to 'make' a mobility hub in a suitable location. Maybe even just some smaller-sized leaflets or similar materials handed or post-out to a local community might help towards shifting travel behaviours towards more sustainable modes, and encourage those who can to make more use of what mobility services are already offered at a local level.
